title: Hello
scope: Whole phrases only, learned by ear; no grammar is taught yet. Polite (-aṇḍi / mīru) forms, as used with a partner's parents and elders; the few plain phrases say who they are for.

spans.s: What people say and what books teach

items.s: For thanks and sorry, people at home say the English words, in a Telugu accent. Within a family, thanks is often not said at all.
The Telugu words are formal. They are right for an elder you have just met, and they are what textbooks teach.

spans.s: The word below only denies what something
: "no, it isn't", "no, that's not right". "I don't want it" and "there isn't any" are different words, and they come in Units 5 and 7.
People avoid a bare "I'm going": it sounds final. The usual goodbye, said by the person who is leaving, means "I'll go and come back".

items.note: Works at any time of day, for arriving and for leaving. Often said with the palms together. You will also hear the shorter namastē, a lot of it in Hyderabad; both are fine.
Word for word: 'are you well?'. The final -ā turns a statement into a yes/no question. You will also hear elā unnāru? ('how are you?'); it is just as common and is answered the same way.
To an elder you can add the respectful ending: bāgunnānaṇḍi.
Used for one person you respect, and for any group of people. The close-friend 'you' comes in Unit 4.

en_alt: I'm fine, and how are you?

items.note: 'Yes' with the respectful ending -aṇḍi. This is the one to use with elders.
Only denies what something is. 'I don't want' and 'there isn't' are other words (Units 5 and 7).
Said to approve of a plan or of news: 'good', 'that's fine then'.
Many people answer with just the second word. The yes is not wrong; it is a little formal.
sarē with the respectful ending. Between sarē and -aṇḍi an n slips in: sarēnaṇḍi.
Formal. Right for an elder you have just met, a speech, or a letter. At home people say the everyday word.

literary.note: Writing and formal speech use the Telugu word; everyday speech uses the English one.

items.note: The English word, said the Telugu way. This is what most people say day to day.
Word for word: 'please forgive'. A formal apology. It is not normally used to get someone's attention.

literary.note: Writing and formal speech use the Telugu word; everyday speech uses the English one.

items.note: The usual answer to 'sorry' and to 'thanks'. You will see it spelled several ways; all are the same word.
Bare sarē is for someone your own age or younger. To an elder, say sarēnaṇḍi.
parvālēdu with the respectful ending: the final u drops. A polite way to turn down help or an offer.

Word for word: 'to me it didn't become meaning': it didn't make sense to me. People often drop the first word.

literary.note: Written as two words; in speech they run together into one.

items.note: What the person leaving says. A bare 'I'm going' is avoided because it sounds final. When two or more of you leave together, say veḷḷostām ('we'll go and come back').
The word means 'care, caution'. Said by itself to someone who is leaving, mostly to someone your own age or younger, and as a warning: 'careful!'.
What a host says at the door. Often doubled: 'raṇḍi, raṇḍi'.
